segments.text: The birthday paradox.
segments.caption: The birthday paradox.

segments.text: Why your gut gets it wrong, the maths step by step, a live simulation, and where it's used in real life. Save this one!
segments.caption: Why your gut gets it wrong, the maths step by step, a live simulation, and where it's used in real life. Save this one!

segments.text: A cricket match. Twenty-two players on the field, plus the umpire. Twenty-three people.
segments.caption: A cricket match. 22 players on the field, plus the umpire. 23 people.

segments.text: What's the chance that two of them share a birthday?
segments.caption: What's the chance that two of them share a birthday?

segments.text: Most people guess around six percent. Twenty-three out of three sixty-five. Comment your guess before the answer.
segments.caption: Most people guess around 6%. 23 out of 365. Comment your guess before the answer.

segments.text: The real answer? 50.7 percent. Basically a coin flip.
segments.caption: The real answer? 50.7%. Basically a coin flip.

segments.text: And with seventy people, it's 99.9 percent. Almost certain.
segments.caption: And with 70 people, it's 99.9%. Almost certain.

segments.text: Your brain is answering the wrong question. It's thinking: does someone share my birthday?
segments.caption: Your brain is answering the wrong question. It's thinking: does someone share my birthday?

segments.text: That really is small: about six percent.
segments.caption: That really is small: about 6%.

segments.text: But the question is: do any two people share a birthday? And with twenty-three people, there are two hundred and fifty-three different pairs.
segments.caption: But the question is: do ANY two people share a birthday? And with 23 people, there are 253 different pairs.

segments.text: Even five friends make ten pairs. Every new person pairs up with everyone already in the room.
segments.caption: Even 5 friends make 10 pairs. Every new person pairs up with everyone already in the room.

segments.text: That's two hundred and fifty-three chances for a match.
segments.caption: That's 253 chances for a match.

segments.text: It's easier to work out the opposite: everyone has a different birthday.
segments.caption: It's easier to work out the opposite: everyone has a different birthday.

segments.text: Person one can have any day: three sixty-five out of three sixty-five.
segments.caption: Person 1 can have any day: 365 out of 365.

segments.text: Person two must avoid that day: three sixty-four out of three sixty-five.
segments.caption: Person 2 must avoid that day: 364 out of 365.

segments.text: Person three: three sixty-three out of three sixty-five. And so on, down to person twenty-three: three forty-three out of three sixty-five.
segments.caption: Person 3: 363 out of 365. And so on, down to person 23: 343 out of 365.

segments.text: Each fraction is only a little below one. But multiply twenty-two of them, and the total shrinks fast.
segments.caption: Each fraction is only a little below 1. But multiply 22 of them, and the total shrinks fast.

segments.text: Multiply them all, and the chance that everyone is different is only 49.3 percent.
segments.caption: Multiply them all, and the chance that everyone is different is only 49.3%.

segments.text: So the chance of at least one shared birthday is a hundred minus 49.3: that's 50.7 percent.
segments.caption: So the chance of at least one shared birthday is 100 minus 49.3: that's 50.7%.

segments.text: Watch how fast it climbs.
segments.caption: Watch how fast it climbs.

segments.text: Ten people: twelve percent. Twenty-three people: fifty. Forty people: eighty-nine. Fifty-seven people: ninety-nine percent.
segments.caption: 10 people: 12%. 23 people: 50%. 40 people: 89%. 57 people: 99%.

segments.text: Still don't believe it? We simulated a thousand rooms, each with twenty-three random people.
segments.caption: Still don't believe it? We simulated 1,000 rooms, each with 23 random people.

segments.text: In five hundred and seven of them, two people shared a birthday. Half the rooms, just like the maths said.
segments.caption: In 507 of them, two people shared a birthday. Half the rooms, just like the maths said.

segments.text: And this isn't just a party trick.
segments.caption: And this isn't just a party trick.

segments.text: Hackers use it. The birthday attack finds two files with the same digital fingerprint much faster than you'd expect. That's why passwords and bank systems use extremely long codes.
segments.caption: Hackers use it. The birthday attack finds two files with the same digital fingerprint much faster than you'd expect. That's why passwords and bank systems use extremely long codes.

segments.text: And in a class of sixty students? A shared birthday is 99.4 percent certain.
segments.caption: And in a class of 60 students? A shared birthday is 99.4% certain.

segments.text: So remember: when everyone is compared with everyone, the pairs explode, and coincidences become likely.
segments.caption: So remember: when everyone is compared with everyone, the pairs explode, and coincidences become likely.

segments.text: It's also why lottery results seem to repeat suspiciously often. With enough draws, a repeat is expected.
segments.caption: It's also why lottery results seem to repeat suspiciously often. With enough draws, a repeat is expected.
